title: Grief and the Will
hookLine: bhaana lets grief sit alongside trust
tomorrow: there's no grave to visit. so where does Simran go?

cards: Sympathy cards have a handful of stock lines, and Simran has now heard every one. The worst comes in the locker room.
A teammate, meaning well, squeezes her arm: it was God's will, he's in a better place, everything happens for a reason. Simran says thanks. In the car she texts Maya a row of screaming faces.
She knows the word for God's will. Bebe says it at every meal. So why does it land like a slap when someone else says it?

teach.b: The Sikh word is bhaana: the Will, and the trust that whatever happens is held inside it.

Japji opens the question on its first page, Ang 1, asking, in paraphrase: how do we become true, how does the wall of falsehood break? The answer is to walk in the hukam, the Command, which is written with you.
And Guru Arjan, in Raag Asa, Ang 394, says it as a prayer of trust, in paraphrase: whatever You do feels sweet to me.

teach.h: SAID OF YOUR OWN LIFE, NOT AT OTHERS.
teach.b: Here's what the slogan gets wrong, and it's worth telling a friend tonight: bhaana in Gurbani is something a person grows into and says about their own life, not a line handed to someone else to end their sadness.
Guru Arjan's line is a person speaking for himself. Bebe says tera bhaana meetha lage, your will is sweet, while she's still wiping her eyes.
Trust and tears in the same breath, neither one canceling the other. That's what the teammate skipped. Simran doesn't owe anyone a reason.
She can say, I trust the Will, and I miss him, and both halves are true.

how: Sikhs speak of accepting bhaana, the Will, in loss, often saying 'tera bhaana meetha lage' (your will is sweet); the antim ardas asks for the strength to accept it, and mourners are comforted with Gurbani rather than explanations.

games.q: what does “grief and the will” mean?
o: believing every death has a reason you can know
praying until the sadness has completely gone
trusting the Will while still allowed to grieve

games.q: trust beside grief — tap the pairs.
p: the Will, and trust in it
says it while wiping her eyes

s: accepting God's will means you shouldn't feel sad
Bebe says the Will is sweet while still crying; trust and tears sit together.
Japji's first page speaks of walking in the hukam
Ang 1: walk in the Command, written with you.
'everything happens for a reason' is a line from the Granth
a popular saying; Gurbani speaks of trust you grow into, not a reason handed out.

games.q: your friend's dog died, and you want to comfort her. you've been learning about bhaana. what do you say?
o: it was meant to be; everything happens for a reason.
i'm so sorry. you loved him. i'm here.
at least he had a long life, so don't be too sad.
games.why: bhaana is something you grow into for yourself, not a line to hand someone else. comfort first; trust is hers to find.

practice: Take a pen and write two short lines, one under the other. First, something you've lost, in a few words. Under it: and still.
Leave the second line unfinished, or finish it if you can. Both lines stay on the page together.

wordCard.voice: Grief and the Will. Bhaana is trust that what happens is held in the Will; it sits beside grief and doesn't erase it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhaana, the Will; what pleases God, and the trust that accepts it.

carryVoice: Carry this: in his will, and still allowed to miss him, both halves true. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Japji, pauri 1: 'hukam rajaaee chalnaa nanak likhiaa naal'), paraphrased
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394 (Raag Asa, Guru Arjan: 'tera keeaa meethaa laagai'), paraphrased
